hyperedges.label: Release Automation Flow (Conventional Commits to Binaries)

nodes.label: Dependabot Configuration
nodes.rationale: Action versions and NuGet packages go stale quietly; monthly grouped updates with chore-prefixed commits are the thing that notices.

nodes.label: CI Workflow (three-OS build)
nodes.rationale: Builds on ubuntu/windows/macos with -warnaserror, deliberately: a warning allowed to accumulate is a warning nobody reads. The test step says out loud that no test project exists yet rather than letting a green check imply the code was tested.

nodes.label: Release Please Workflow
nodes.rationale: Derives SemVer from Conventional Commits; every push to main opens/updates a release PR (CHANGELOG + version) and merging it creates the tag and release. A tag created with the default GITHUB_TOKEN deliberately does not trigger the tag-push workflow (GitHub's recursion guard), so binaries are attached by calling the release workflow via workflow_call.

nodes.label: Release Workflow (single-file binaries)
nodes.rationale: Cross-publishes win-x64/linux-x64/osx-arm64 from Linux because the builds use neither ReadyToRun nor build-time signing; the assembly version comes from the tag. SignPath Authenticode steps skip themselves until the repository variables and secret exist so releases keep working unsigned. Checksums are computed after signing on purpose: they must describe the bytes people actually download.

nodes.label: Management Tab (viewAdmin / Yönetim)
nodes.rationale: Declares up front that it does not carry the migration's guarantees — nothing runs in a transaction, nothing rolls back, a dropped database is gone. Drop dialog requires typing the name back and offers ownership reassignment; generated passwords are shown once in a dialog that says they were stored nowhere.

nodes.label: Migrator Page (index.html, Turkish UI)
nodes.rationale: The single Turkish page: saved servers, source picker with filter, target pattern/collation, option groups (run mode radios, mirror, ORM history overwrite flag, gate-opening relaxed checks marked 'kapı açar', per-database users), live log, PDF report button. The theme is applied before first paint so a chosen theme never flashes the other; dialogs use native <dialog> for focus trapping, Esc and backdrop with no library and no build step.

nodes.label: verify-ui Skill (Playwright UI Audit)
nodes.rationale: The UI has no build step and no test project, and the failures that matter render as a page that looks fine: a colour a tenth of a point under WCAG AA, an id app.js reaches for after a rename, a hidden attribute defeated by a display rule. The skill measures those instead — id wiring, labels, resolved-background contrast, focus ring, overflow at 390/768/1280px, console errors — in both themes. Playwright lives in the skill's own package.json so the shipped app keeps zero JS dependencies. Contrast fixes go in the token, not the call site.

nodes.label: Conventional Commits
nodes.rationale: Required because release-please derives the SemVer version and changelog from the commit history: feat bumps minor, fix bumps patch, feat!/BREAKING CHANGE bumps major.

nodes.label: IServerAdmin Seam (PostgresAdmin / SqlServerAdmin)
nodes.rationale: A real interface rather than a file-layout seam, because there were two implementations from the start — the roadmap's reason for not extracting the engine's seam yet does not apply here.

nodes.label: Nine-Step Migration Pipeline
nodes.rationale: A run is a fixed sequence — collation check, schema read, plan, source-only check, pre-flight, copy, sequence fixup, verify, commit — and every step can stop the run, because stopping is always safer than continuing.

nodes.label: Migrator.Core/Admin Separation
nodes.rationale: Admin lives in Migrator.Core only because that is where product-specific SQL lives and Migrator.App has none. It is not part of the engine, is unreachable from MigrationEngine, and none of the migration guarantees apply to it — it exists to create, alter and drop things, the opposite of what the engine promises, and separate namespaces keep that distinction from blurring.

nodes.label: Provider Seam (Source Reader / Target Writer)
nodes.rationale: The engine is written against two roles — a source reader and a target writer — filled today by concrete SQL Server and PostgreSQL code (SchemaReader, TargetDatabase, MigrationEngine.WriteValueAsync). The seam lives in file layout rather than interfaces because an abstraction extracted from a single implementation is a guess.

nodes.label: Any SQL to Any SQL Goal
nodes.norm_label: any sql to any sql goal
nodes.rationale: SQL Server to PostgreSQL is the first pair because it was needed first, not because the tool is about those products. Product-specific code is isolated; everything about migrating safely is shared and stays shared.

nodes.label: The Escape Hatches (Relaxable Checks)
nodes.rationale: Four checks can be turned off — allow tables missing from target, allow schema risk, allow collation mismatch, verify only. All are off by default, each exists because a real migration occasionally needs it, and each says what it lets through. Turning one on without reading what it reported cancels the reason the tool exists.

nodes.label: Generated Passwords Exist Only in the PDF
nodes.norm_label: generated passwords exist only in the pdf
nodes.rationale: Per-database passwords are generated in memory, written into the PDF report, and held only until the process exits — never stored in the connections file, a log or a temp file. Nobody can recover them from the machine, including the user: if the report is lost the password must be reset with ALTER ROLE. The PDF is a credential.

nodes.label: Server Management Panel (No Migration Guarantees)
nodes.rationale: A different tool that happens to live in the same window: nothing is transactional, nothing reversible. Instead: a drop names its cost first, only proceeds when the object's name is typed back (checked server-side too), system objects are refused outright, closing other sessions is opt-in, blocked deletes explain themselves and offer ownership reassignment, and the server's own error DETAIL is shown verbatim.

nodes.label: Stored Credentials (Machine-Keyed DataProtection)
nodes.rationale: Saved connections live in a local JSON file with passwords encrypted via ASP.NET Core data-protection keys scoped to the machine — the file is not portable. This protects the file at rest and against accidental commits, not against someone already logged in as the user, because the app must decrypt to connect.

nodes.label: Mirror Missing Tables Option
nodes.rationale: Creates tables the target lacks from the source schema — columns, NOT NULL, identity, primary and foreign keys — but not defaults, indexes or check constraints, so it is a fast stand-up, not a substitute for ORM migrations. It never creates an ORM history table and never mirrors rowversion, because a bytea NOT NULL column nothing can fill would make every application insert fail after a verified migration.

nodes.label: One User per Database Option
nodes.rationale: After a database migrates, a PostgreSQL login role with a 24-character random password is created from a {db}_user pattern and made owner of the database and its public schema. An existing role is reused and its password is not rotated, because something is probably already using it. CONNECT is revoked from PUBLIC only for databases this run created.

nodes.label: Run Modes (Migrate / VerifyOnly / ProvisionOnly)
nodes.rationale: Three exclusive modes; options a mode would ignore are locked on the page with the reason, because showing them as available promised work that never happened. Verify only writes nothing at all; create-database-only opens the source anyway because a target named after a nonexistent source is a typo, not a plan, and a run that made the database but not the requested login is reported as failed.

nodes.label: SQL Data Migrator
nodes.rationale: Exists because one-off migration scripts share three flaws: they report success they did not earn, they leave a half-loaded target on failure, and they move rows without re-validating constraints. All three are avoidable and cost real money.

nodes.label: Verification Defeat Treated as Security Issue
nodes.norm_label: verification defeat treated as security issue
nodes.rationale: Verification is the guarantee the tool is built around; a way to make a migration pass verification while the data is wrong is classified as a security issue, not just a bug.

nodes.label: .claude Configuration Directory
nodes.rationale: Checked in so every human or agent gets the same conventions and verification tools; deleting it loses only the guardrails. No secrets may be added — it is a public repository — and there is deliberately no .mcp.json because everything needed is reachable through the .NET SDK, docker and gh.

nodes.label: Contributor Covenant Code of Conduct v2.1
nodes.norm_label: contributor covenant code of conduct v2.1

nodes.label: Interface Palette (Contrast-Mapped Teal Set)
nodes.rationale: The palette (#88BDBC, #254E58, #112D32, #4F4A41, #6E6658) was chosen by the maintainer and mapped to interface roles by contrast measurement rather than by eye; the reasoning lives in the token block of style.css. The durable output of the one-off design session is the CSS plus the committed verify-ui skill that enforces its conclusions on every change.

nodes.label: What the Engine Is Not Allowed to Do
nodes.norm_label: what the engine is not allowed to do
nodes.rationale: Never report success it did not earn; never leave a half-migrated target; never relax a check by default. A change that makes a run more likely to appear to succeed is a change in the wrong direction, however convenient.

nodes.label: English Code / Turkish UI Split
nodes.rationale: Code, comments, commits, docs and engine log text are English; anything a user reads on the page is Turkish, including wwwroot/index.html, the TR dictionary in app.js, and the PDF report strings even though they live in C#.

nodes.label: Message Codes as Wire Format
nodes.rationale: The engine never formats a sentence for a user: it reports English Text plus a stable Code and Args, and the browser translates by code via the TR map in app.js. A missing TR entry silently falls back to English; renaming a code silently drops its translation, so codes are added, never repurposed. Engine codes (Migrator.Core/MessageCode.cs) are kept apart from application codes (Migrator.App/AppMessageCode.cs) because a batch is not something the engine knows about.

nodes.label: No-Build-Step Embedded UI
nodes.rationale: wwwroot is plain HTML/CSS/JS embedded into the assembly so the published single-file executable carries its own interface. No CDN, no external fonts, no npm — the app is offline and localhost-only. The PDF report ships its own font (Assets/DejaVuSans.ttf) so Turkish letters render on a machine with no fonts installed.

nodes.label: No Test Project (Announced Gap)
nodes.rationale: CI says on every run that nothing was tested rather than hiding the gap behind a green check; the engine was deliberately built with no console and no HTTP so a future test harness can drive it. CI already looks for tests/*/*.csproj.

nodes.label: Verification Before Commit (Single Transaction)
nodes.rationale: Steps 6 through 9 (truncate+copy, sequence fixup, verify, commit) share one transaction — the load-bearing decision of the codebase. Verifying after the commit would detect problems and leave them in place, producing a failure report next to committed bad data, which is worse than not checking.

nodes.label: Target-Driven Type Mapping
nodes.rationale: Mapping is driven by the target store type, not the source type, so the table grows with target types instead of the product of source and target. timestamp is written verbatim with DateTimeKind.Unspecified (no UTC shift); timestamptz treats kind-less DateTimes as UTC because the host's timezone is not part of the data. Text is never case-folded — casing is data.

nodes.label: ISourceReader / ITargetWriter Extraction (Roadmap Item 1)
nodes.rationale: Promoting the provider seam to interfaces comes before the second provider on purpose: an abstraction extracted from one implementation is a guess, but one extracted just before the second implementation lands is informed by knowing what actually varies.

nodes.label: Local-Only Operation as Security Property
nodes.rationale: The app binds to localhost and holds credentials for production databases. Keeping it local is a security property, not a limitation to grow out of; multi-user or hosted operation is a non-goal that looks like a goal.

nodes.label: Deliberately Out of Scope
nodes.rationale: Schema creation/translation, continuous replication and data transformation are different jobs with their own failure modes; conflating any of them with data movement makes both harder to trust. A pull request adding one will be declined no matter how good the code is.

nodes.label: Failure Leaves the Target Untouched
nodes.rationale: The truncate, the copy, the sequence fixup and the verification share one transaction; if any fails, the rollback leaves the target byte-identical to what it was before the run. There is never a half-migrated state to clean up.

nodes.label: CASCADE Closure Computed Before Locks
nodes.rationale: TRUNCATE ... RESTART IDENTITY CASCADE reaches every target table referencing one being copied; the affected set is computed from the target's foreign keys and listed during pre-flight, before the transaction opens. The check also proves history-table preservation: if a preserved table falls inside the cascade closure the run fails, naming the table and the foreign-key path — a guarantee is not built on 'safe in practice, unverified in principle'.

nodes.label: Identifier Quoting per Product
nodes.rationale: No SQL dialect accepts a bound parameter where an identifier goes, so names from the browser are quoted for their product (double-quote doubled for PostgreSQL, bracket doubled for SQL Server) and rejected if they carry a control character. A SQL Server collation name sits in a keyword position and cannot be quoted, so it is validated against letters, digits and underscores instead.

nodes.label: ORM Migration History Is the Target's and Is Kept
nodes.norm_label: orm migration history is the target's and is kept
nodes.rationale: History tables (__EFMigrationsHistory, django_migrations, schema_migrations, flyway_schema_history, __drizzle_migrations) describe the target, not the data being moved, so they are neither truncated nor filled. Copying the source's rows replaces a true statement with a false one: EF finds no baseline record, re-applies it, and fails on existing tables — a real failure this tool once caused. Mirroring never creates a history table, and copying history anyway is an explicit overwrite option, not a relaxed check.

nodes.label: Source Is Read-Only in a Migration
nodes.norm_label: source is read-only in a migration
nodes.rationale: Every statement a migration sends to the source is a SELECT, which makes rollback trivial: point the application back at the source and nothing has been lost. The promise was deliberately narrowed from 'the source is never written to' when the management panel arrived, because the app as a whole can now administer any registered server and saying otherwise would be untrue.

nodes.label: Success Means the Data Actually Moved
nodes.norm_label: success means the data actually moved
nodes.rationale: A run only exits successfully if the copy plan was non-empty, at least one row was copied, every table's row count matches the source, and no foreign key has an orphaned child row. Any of those failing is a failure, not a warning. FKs are re-checked because constraint triggers are suspended during the copy.

nodes.label: Localhost Trust Boundary
nodes.rationale: The local API has no authentication by design: it binds to localhost and the security boundary is the machine and the user account. Treating a local tool as multi-user would mean pretending it is a service. Anything that defeats the localhost boundary is a vulnerability.
